query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: If a partially sintered tungsten (W) preform is infiltrated with molten copper (Cu) under hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at ≥100 MPa and 1100–1200 °C in an inert atmosphere, the resulting W–Cu composite will exhibit reduced porosity, fewer interfacial defects, and improved mechanical durability compared to W–Cu materials fabricated by conventional infiltration or spark-plasma sintering.
generation.material_initial_state: Partially sintered tungsten skeleton or connected W regions
generation.intervention: High-pressure copper infiltration via hot isostatic pressing
generation.conditions: ≥100 MPa at 1100–1200 °C in an inert environment
generation.structural_mediator: Near-complete infiltration and densification of the W skeleton by Cu under high hydrostatic pressure
generation.mechanism: Applied pressure forces molten Cu into any residual pores and promotes strong interfacial bonding, mitigating phase separation and void formation to yield a dense, mechanically robust composite microstructure
generation.predicted_outcome: A more homogeneous W–Cu composite with superior mechanical strength, reduced defect levels, and higher thermal conductivity under operational stress compared to conventional infiltration or SPS routes
generation.baseline: Standard infiltration or spark-plasma sintering processes that often leave residual pores or inhomogeneous W–Cu distributions
generation.boundary: The process is currently demonstrated at laboratory scale only; feasibility of large-scale industrial implementation and in-reactor performance must still be validated
generation.uncertainty: Residual stresses and possible interfacial reactions under large infiltration pressures are not fully characterized and may limit the consistency of the final microstructure

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites, one using the proposed HIP infiltration method at 1100–1200 °C and ≥100 MPa, and another using a conventional infiltration or SPS approach. Assess density, interfacial bonding, and mechanical performance.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (porosity, grain boundaries) using optical or electron microscopy
Room-temperature tensile/compression testing to evaluate strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HIP-infiltrated composite does not have significantly lower porosity, fails to show improved mechanical properties, or does not exhibit higher thermal conductivity compared to the baseline methods, the hypothesis is falsified.
